Years 11–13 Social Sciences

Learning expectations
Through Social Sciences, students develop the knowledge, capabilities, and analytical skills
needed to understand people, societies, cultures, environments, institutions, and ideas. They are
taught methods to investigate questions, evaluate evidence, examine patterns and data, consider
diverse perspectives, construct arguments, and communicate well-reasoned conclusions.
The learning area supports students to engage critically with a range of historical and
contemporary issues and participate thoughtfully in local, national, and global communities.


Key features of the refreshed learning area
•     Four new New Zealand Curriculum (NZC) subjects: Civics, Politics, and Philosophy; Pacific
      Studies; Sociology; and Te Ao Māori.
•     Shared NZC and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa (TMOA) pathways in Geography | Matawhenua
      and History | Te Takanga o te Wā.
•     Explicit teaching of disciplinary writing, helping students develop and apply discipline-specific
      writing conventions within each social science subject.
•     Strong connections between disciplinary learning and authentic real-world contexts, including
      social, cultural, environmental, political, and economic issues and challenges.
•     Clear teaching sequences and curriculum guidance, including specified contexts, case studies,
      and examples where appropriate.
•     Explicit use of disciplinary concepts, theories, frameworks, and methods to investigate and
      explain human behaviour, societies, cultures, environments, and historical change.


Subjects
Subjects within the learning area are:

•     Years 12–13 Civics, Politics, and Philosophy
•     Years 12–13 Classical Studies
•     Years 11–13 Geography
•     Years 11–13 History
•     Years 12–13 Pacific Studies 1

Learning and pathways

Years 12–13 Civics, Politics, and Philosophy
Students are taught civic, political, and philosophical concepts, including argument, evidence,
ethical frameworks, political theories, civic institutions, and systems of thought. They apply
disciplinary frameworks and practices to interpret and evaluate evidence, analyse issues and
perspectives, develop well-reasoned arguments, and make justified judgements about questions of
knowledge, justice, authority, rights, power, and public life.

Strands

Years 12–13 Civics, Politics, and Philosophy is organised into three subject strands and a
disciplinary writing strand:

•   Truth, Evidence, and Argument
•   Morality, Legality, and Justice
•   Sovereignty, Authority, and Autonomy
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Civics, Politics, and Philosophy leads to pathways in civics, politics, and philosophy
and related fields, such as public policy, governance, international relations, diplomacy, and law.


Years 12–13 Classical Studies
Students are taught about the literature, art and architecture, societies, belief systems, and
historical evidence of Classical Greece and Rome. They apply disciplinary concepts and practices
to analyse primary sources, evaluate interpretations and perspectives, and construct evidence-
based judgements about the classical world and its influence across time, place, and cultures.

Strands

Years 12–13 Classical Studies is organised into four subject strands and a disciplinary writing
strand:

•   Literature and Narrative
•   Art and Architecture
•   Society and History
•   Interrelationship of Classical Knowledges
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Classical Studies leads to pathways in Classical Studies and related disciplines, such
as humanities, history, philosophy, archaeology, and law.


Years 11–13 Geography
Students are taught about people, places, and environments, and the connections between them
at local, national, and global scales. They use geographic concepts, evidence, and geospatial tools
to investigate spatial patterns and processes, evaluate geographic issues and responses, and
communicate informed conclusions about environmental and societal challenges.

Strands

Years 11–13 Geography is organised into three subject strands and a disciplinary writing strand:

•   Physical Geography
•   Human Geography
•   Geographic Investigation
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 11–13 Geography leads to pathways in geography and related fields, including
environmental and climate sciences, conservation and resource management, urban and regional
planning, geospatial technologies (GIS), hazard and emergency management, public policy, and
international development.

History
Students are taught about significant historical events, movements, places, and figures that have
influenced New Zealand, the Pacific, and the world. Students are taught how to use practices of
history, such as interpreting primary and secondary sources, constructing and contesting
narratives, and applying evidence to explain the past. Students are taught how historical
interpretations and perspectives are used to explain the past and establish historical significance.




Years 11–13 Social Sciences InfoSheet | October 2026                                              3 of 6

Strands

Years 11–13 History is organised into four subject strands and a disciplinary writing strand:

•   Historical Methods
•   Historical Narrative and Interpretation
•   Historical Relationships
•   Historical Significance
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

History leads to pathways in history, humanities, social sciences, education, law, public policy,
journalism, international relations, and related fields.


Years 12–13 Psychology
Students explore psychological concepts, theories, approaches, and research methodologies to
explain behaviour and mental processes. They examine biological, social, environmental, and
cultural influences, and use evidence-based inquiry to evaluate psychological claims and
explanations, including ethical considerations in psychological research.

Strands

Years 12–13 Psychology is organised into four subject strands and a disciplinary writing strand:

•   Research Methodologies
•   Biopsychology
•   Cognitive Psychology
•   Sociocultural Psychology
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 12–13 Psychology leads to pathways in psychology and related disciplines such as health
sciences, law, education, and commerce.


Years 11–13 Religious Studies
Students are taught about religious and spiritual worldviews, and how beliefs, practices, traditions,
texts, histories, and ethical systems shape identity, meaning, ethics, and society. They analyse and
apply understandings of religious information in real-world and theoretical contexts, evaluate
diverse perspectives, and communicate evidence-based judgements grounded in a broader
understanding of justice, human dignity, and religious diversity.




Years 11–13 Social Sciences InfoSheet | October 2026                                                4 of 6

Strands

Years 11–13 Religious Studies is organised into four subject strands and a disciplinary writing
strand:

•   Religious Beliefs and Practices
•   Religious Narratives
•   Religious History
•   Religious Ethics
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 11–13 Religious Studies leads to pathways in humanities, law, education, and
international relations.


Years 11–13 Sociology
Students are taught sociological concepts, theories, frameworks, and research practices used to
understand social behaviour, relationships, social institutions, identities, and social structures. They
apply sociological reasoning and evidence to analyse social issues and patterns, evaluate
competing explanations, and develop informed understandings of how culture, power, and social
structures shape societies and human behaviour.

Strands

Years 11–13 Sociology is organised into three subject strands and a disciplinary writing strand:

•   Social Theories and Sociological Research
•   Society, Culture, and Identity
•   Social Institutions
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Years 11–13 Sociology leads to pathways in sociology and related disciplines, such as social
policy, education, criminology, politics, and media.

Te Ao Māori
Students are taught about the development of both individual and collective Māori identity,
belonging, and relationships; Māori conceptual thinking; Māori knowledge systems; and tikanga
Māori. Students are also taught about leadership, enterprise, Māori voice, and connections to
people and place including global connections. Students will examine how historical and
contemporary experiences influence Māori identity and belonging, and their aspirations for future
generations to adapt and flourish in a changing world.

Strands

Years 11–13 Te Ao Māori is organised into three subject strands and a disciplinary writing strand:

•   Identity Relationships, Belonging
•   Leadership, Responsibility, and Enterprise
•   Continuity, Knowledge, and Enterprise
•   Disciplinary Writing.

Pathways

Te Ao Māori leads to pathways across many sectors including cultural, business, enterprise,
education, law, art, media, creative industries, policy, and resource management.


Connections to other learning areas
Social Sciences connects strongly with:

•   English through disciplinary reading, writing, communication, argumentation, and the
    interpretation of texts, perspectives, and evidence
•   Mathematics through investigations, data analysis, graphing, demographics, and quantitative
    reasoning, patterns, and modelling
•   Science through sustainability, climate change and action, environmental issues, human-
    environment interactions, biological functions, and evidence-based inquiry
•   Technology through digital citizenship, communication technologies, and understanding the
    impacts of technological change and innovation on people and societies
•   Health and Physical Education through relationships, culture, identity, participation, and
    individual and social influences on behaviour.


How to design a programme
Teachers designing programmes should have a clear overview of the full curriculum for their
subject, including the teaching sequence and any accompanying specifications, context
requirements, case studies, depth studies, or other curriculum requirements. Programmes should
be deliberately planned to provide coverage, coherence, and progression within and across each
year. Different Social Sciences subjects have distinctive approaches to programme design and
sequencing, which should be carefully read. Teachers should use the subject-specific teaching
sequence guidance to support decisions about how learning is organised and integrated within
their programme.
